subject: Biology
title: Why Flu Needs a New Vaccine Every Year
description: A 60-second lesson on Why Flu Needs a New Vaccine Every Year.

hook.text: You get a flu shot every year—but one measles vaccine lasts a lifetime. Why the difference?

buildup.text: Influenza mutates rapidly. Its surface proteins shift every season, disguising it from memory cells.

discovery.text: Antigenic drift causes small mutations. Antigenic shift mixes genes from different flu strains entirely.

twist.text: The 1918 flu pandemic killed 50 million people—an antigenic shift created a strain nobody was immune to.

climax.text: Scientists predict next year's dominant strains and update the vaccine each year—sometimes they guess wrong.

punchline.text: Same enemy, new disguise. Every single year.

quiz.question: Why must the flu vaccine be updated annually?
options: The virus mutates rapidly, changing its surface proteins
The vaccine wears off after a year

details.summary: Influenza requires annual vaccination because the virus mutates rapidly through antigenic drift, small mutations accumulating in surface proteins, and antigenic shift, major reassortment when different flu strains combine. Last year's immune memory no longer matches the new strain.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding flu evolution explains why influenza kills 290,000 to 650,000 people annually despite available vaccines. It also explains why pandemic preparedness requires constant surveillance and why universal flu vaccines are a major research p...
takeaways: Antigenic drift causes small mutations that gradually change surface proteins
Antigenic shift creates entirely new strains when different viruses recombine
WHO monitors global flu strains to predict which to include in each year's vaccine

faq.question: What is the difference between antigenic drift and antigenic shift?
faq.answer: Antigenic drift involves gradual accumulation of small mutations in surface proteins, requiring annual vaccine updates. Antigenic shift occurs when entirely different flu subtypes combine, creating novel viruses with pandemic potential. The 2009 H1N1 pandemic resulted from antigenic shift.

faq.question: How do scientists predict which flu strains to include in the vaccine?
faq.answer: The WHO coordinates a global surveillance network monitoring flu strains in both hemispheres year-round. Scientists analyze trends in circulating strains and predict which will dominate the next season. Predictions must be made months ahead, which is why accuracy varies annually.
